fixes.explanation: Terrified is right, baker. The text says Moab was terrified of the people because they were numerous, and then adds, “Indeed, Moab dreaded the Israelites.” (Numbers 22:3) Terrified and dreaded, back to back. That's a whole nation checking the locks.

Pethor by the Euphrates, yes. The text says Balak sent messengers to summon Balaam at Pethor, “…which is by the Euphrates in the land of his people.” (Numbers 22:5) So the messengers had a clear address to head for. They also carried a summons from a king.

Good guess, friend, but Joppa isn't the address in this verse. The text puts Balaam at Pethor, “…which is by the Euphrates in the land of his people.” (Numbers 22:5) The messengers are looking for a man by a river, not a man by the sea.

Close, but Bethel isn't on Balak's list this time. The text says Balaam is at Pethor, “…which is by the Euphrates in the land of his people.” (Numbers 22:5) That's the name the messengers are given, and it's the one to remember.

Blessed is it, baker. God tells Balaam, “Do not go with them. You are not to curse this people, for they are blessed.” (Numbers 22:12) Balak asked for a curse. God's answer comes with a reason, and the reason is that this people are blessed.

Honor him richly, yes. This is Balak's message, carried by the new princes: “…for I will honor you richly and do whatever you say.” (Numbers 22:17) Balak is the one making the promise. He's gone from asking to promising, and I bet Balaam's ears perked up.

That's it, baker. God says, “Since these men have come to summon you, get up and go with them, but you must only do what I tell you.” (Numbers 22:20) Go, with one condition attached. Hold on to that “but,” because God put it right there in the sentence.

That would be dramatic, but it isn't in the text. When the donkey sees the angel of the LORD, “…she turned off the path and went into a field.” (Numbers 22:23) Balaam stays on her, and the text says he beats her to return her to the path. She goes into a field, and he's the one doing the beating.

Down she goes, baker. The text says the donkey “…lay down under Balaam, and he became furious and beat her with his staff.” (Numbers 22:27) That's a rider whose ride just parked itself. Balaam is furious, and the donkey is the one who has seen the angel.

That's the one, baker. The text says, “Then the LORD opened the donkey’s mouth…” (Numbers 22:28) It's the LORD who does it. Then she asks Balaam what she has done to him that he has beaten her these three times.

Not the staff, friend. After Balaam beats the donkey with it, the text says, “Then the LORD opened the donkey’s mouth…” (Numbers 22:28) The LORD isn't acting on the staff. He's acting on the donkey's mouth, and she speaks to Balaam.
No storm, friend. The text says, “Then the LORD opened the donkey’s mouth…” (Numbers 22:28) He doesn't send weather. He opens a mouth, and the donkey speaks to Balaam.

Sinned is right, baker. Balaam bows low and falls facedown, the angel of the LORD asks why he has beaten his donkey, and then Balaam answers, “I have sinned…” (Numbers 22:31–34) He goes on, “…for I did not realize that you were standing in the road to confront me.” (Numbers 22:34) Earlier he told the donkey he'd kill her if he had a sword (Numbers 22:29). Now he's the one owning up.

Not this time, friend. Balaam bows low and falls facedown, and the angel of the LORD asks why he has beaten his donkey these three times. (Numbers 22:31–32) Only then does Balaam answer, “I have sinned…” (Numbers 22:34) It's a short, honest line, and it comes after the angel speaks.
